newsitem.title: UK: London gold fixes at fresh low, but $380 holds.
newsitem.headline: London gold fixes at fresh low, but $380 holds.

text.p: Bullion prices were holding above the key $380.00 per ounce level on Friday but would have to go lower before physical demand was stimulated, dealers said.
Gold was fixed at $380.30 per ounce after $380.45 on Thursday, a fresh low since September 6 last year.
"There was been no sign of real buying so far today at $380.00. In fact, if anything gold is looking a little top heavy," one dealer said.
Others claimed that Middle East origin buying had come into the market already to prop prices around $380.00.
"There was a little on Thursday," another dealer said.
Gold's price fall began on Thursday after investment funds disillusioned by the market's lack of progress began to sell. Extra pressure came with the OTC option expiry, dealers said.

The price fall continued on an announcement from Internatioal Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Michel Camdessus that the IMF had the needed majority to sell five million ounces from its reserves to help the poorest nations.
"It (the gold sale) is in the price already," a dealer said.
Another warned that as long as the IMF issue held over the market, gold's chances of making much progress to the upside were severely limited.
The support around $380.00 held despite some dealers forecasting that gold would fall to $378.00 or even lower before bouncing.
Lease rates crept up in some centres, indicating fresh physical interest coming into the market at the lower prices.
Dealers also had mixed views on the tensions in the Middle East, with some reasoning that buying would be stimulated by the escalating violence between Israelis and Palestinians.
However, another dealer commented, "Tensions have been around in various places for some time but, unfortunately for the markets, gold has not been influenced at all."
Silver opened unchanged but later lost about three cents to $4.85/$4.87. Dealers forecast it slipping to around $4.83 before attracting substantial fresh interest.
"It's oversold and could turn around more quickly than the others when the market changes," one dealer said.
There was less optimism on platinum's medium term outlook.
It fixed at a fresh low since January 31, 1994 at $383.75, down $1.50 from the low going back to the same date set on Thursday. "Investors won't touch it," a dealer said.
